commenti.body:
That’s wild, I just watched this two nights ago for the first time as well, also having it on my watchlist forever. 

I’m a young father too with an 18 month old son and that scene that reveals what happened is haunting. I agree, I don’t know what I’d do man. I was watching it with my girlfriend (his mother) using Plex’s “Watch Together” feature at our separate houses and we both agreed we’d probably kill ourselves a day later if that shit happened to us. Not that that’d be the right thing to do, but it’d just be too heavy to bear it feels like. Unbelievable trauma.

Yeah I came to the conclusion that I couldn't live with that guilt and would end it, but then it's one thing saying it and another doing it. Just a harrowing thing to think about. Casey Affleck 100% deserved the Oscar he got for this film, one of the best acting performances I've seen. It felt like I was watching a real town and real people going through this experience.

Yeah no, I don't even have children and this film destroys me every single time I watch it. 

My \*only\* silly criticism of this would be the use of music, which yes made it more operatic, but also made my wonder what could've been without it in that already HARROWING police station scene in which he begged the police officers to end his life. It's a minor quibble in otherwise nearly flawless execution of story and character. Affleck gave one of the best performances of the 21st century. P E R I O D. 

Not that this needs to happen, nor that he would even approach anything like this film, but like I wonder how Paul Schrader would've handled this particular story considering that Lee is essentially a late career Paul Schrader protagonist, no? lol

I watched Manchester by the Sea a while back. It is funny that you say this. Though I barely remember what it is about I remember walking out of the theater thinking… What a Beautiful movie that was! Yes, feeling that it was just that… perfect! Got to watch it again.

I loved it. It’s become kind of forgotten because Casey Affleck had a #metoo scandal. James Franco, Aziz Ansari, Louis CK, Kevin Spacey… none have recovered from getting canceled. It really brings up an interesting question: do accusations of past sexual crimes taint a film experience for you? Actors have been judged for decades. Fatty Arbuckle. When scandal becomes bigger than star power, can you see beyond it, or is it too distracting?
It really is devastatingly done, isn't it? To me, it's one of those movies like "Secret Sunshine", which I find equally transfixing, but I'm not sure I could make it through a second time.

I saw it when my wife was going through a nightmare pregnancy. We were scared of what the next day would bring…and it hasn’t left me since. I had lost my dad suddenly 5 years before, whose name was Lee. Everything couldn’t be better now. But my heart was broken by that movie in a real weird way.

Had Paul Schrader done it, it would have ended with Lee somehow going to prison and touching his ex-wife's hand through a mirror, signaling some sort of spiritual redemption through self-inflicted punishment.
What I like best about this movie is how it balances the heaviness with levity. There’s some  legitimate funny moments in here but it never feels unearned or out of place. Love this movie.

I agree. Of all the things that movie is, it's also bitingly funny. Examples: the two brief Stentorian scenes. The flashback to the brother in the hospital. The very quick 'I cut my hand' bit. Even the scene with Affleck and his ex meeting on the street. Through the apologies and tears, it's so awkward it's funny, when you know it shouldn't be. On of my favorite movies of the past 20 years. Oh, and the 'Great parenting' bit from the director himself. And Affleck and his nephew trying to find the damn car in the cold.

I love this film. It has a very special place in my heart and I have revisited it on several occasions since I first saw it in the theater. I think what I love about the film is the fact that we don't get the back story until quite late in the film. They just throw us into this guy's banal life and we don't see much special or interesting about him. He works a menial job, lives in a basement apartment, drinks too much and picks fights with people. He doesn't seem interested in much of anything and seems blind to women who are interested in him. 

The film weaves in and out of flashbacks so expertly. We learn about his brother and his heart problem. We learn about his brother's wife and her struggle with alcoholism. And finally, we learn why Lee is living the life he's leading. 

The movie hits so many emotional points: deep sadness, humor, beauty and such tenderness. The part that always makes me break down is after Lee gets his ass kicked at the bar and he wakes up on the couch at his friend's house and his friend's wife embraces him and Lee just breaks down and begins crying. I think it's the only time in the film that we see him cry. It makes me so sad to think about it. It's like the tenderness of a woman is what he's been denying himself since the mistake he made.

I think the film is rewatchable because it's so beautiful. Part of it is the music, which yes, is a little strange and possibly heavy handed at some points, but I think the more you see the film, the more you see the profound beauty of the music. It elevates many of the sequences to almost sacred levels - almost like we're watching a religious or spiritual film, which I suppose it is, in many ways.

But I think what I like most about the film is that the message seems to be that, in the face of grief, life goes on. Despite the grief Lee feels for the loss of his brother, and all the memories it brings back, ultimately, the kid needs a ride to band practice[.](https://dinner.Life)

It's not a silly criticism. Many people didn't like the choice of music, especially in the police station scene. I completely understand why, but personally I loved this choice of music. I think it undercuts the scene - it plays against the genuine emotions in the scene. I think Lonergan does this on purpose for two reasons. 

The Adagio in G minor is one of music's most notorious hoaxes. It was written in the 20th century in a neo-baroque style. Because of this there is an element of phoniness to its character. You can hear it, right? It's beautiful, but at the same time it makes me think of that 'violin' action people do when they're being sarcastic about something sad - when they want to imply 'this story should have violins'. To me, this emphasises Lee's self hatred in this scene. He doesn't want our sympathy, because he doesn't think he deserves it - and there is a strong argument that in this moment he doesn't. The music is almost saying - 'Oh isn't this such a sad scene? Let's all feel bad for this piece of shit who>!got so drunk he burned his kids to death'. !< The music emphasises the tragedy, but at the same time makes us aware of how hatefully pathetic Lee is here. It doesn't deny us feelings of sympathy for him, but it won't allow those feelings to be straight forward. 

The second reason is just to protect the audience. I think without the music this scene would be too much. It allows a a little distance from what we're watching. He reminds us-  'It's just a movie, folks'. It's an act of kindness on his part.
I've never thought about that scene like this but I really like this reading of it.

Interesting. I absolutely love the music in this scene (I hadn’t considered anybody would dislike it, even) but completely disagree on what purpose it is serving. Maybe that’s a good thing though.

The way I see it he very much is deserving of sympathy. Sure he’s a piece of shit a lot of the time, but what happened that night could have happened to anybody.
